# Option B mVPN | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-b-mvpn.md)
.

Load **russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.b.mvpn.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.b.mvpn.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.b.mvpn.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

**NOTE**: This is not working on CSR1000v 16.9.8. You will need to redeploy the topology with CSR100v version 17.x for this to work. This works on 17.3.2 for me.

L3VPN inter-AS option B is fully setup and working. Configure mVPN inter-AS using profile 11 (GRE over P-PIM with BGP C-multicast routing).

*   Use P-PIM in the core with SSM
    
    *   PIM is already enabled everywhere, including on the ASBR NNI links
        
    
*   Use BGP for C-multicast signaling
    
*   BGP ipv4/mvpn is already configured within each AS, but not at the ASBR-ASBR links
    
*   The following links are shutdown:
    
    *   The R8-R13 and R8-R14
        
    *   The R1-XR12
        
        *   Do not use XR12 as a PE for this lab
            
        
    *   The XR11-R3
        
    

On R1, join (192.0.2.1, 232.1.1.1) within VRF L3B and L3C. Ensure that when R1 VRF L3A pings this group, both 172.16.18.1 and 172.16.110.1 respond.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-b-mvpn#ee71a8e0-878d-4cc1-a0f0-ecdc049cf510)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-b-mvpn#id-32cc5ee1-ff0d-4de0-b8e3-6997af4703db)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In inter-AS option A mVPN, the ASBRs treat each other as PEs. They must enable mVPN on the VRF and run PIM with the ASBR. In inter-AS option B mVPN, the ASBRs simply exchange ipv4/mvpn routes. They do not run the customer VRFs.

The PEs run normal mVPN but with some slight modifications to enable inter-as support. First, the PEs must use the **inter-as** keyword so that the no-export community is not included on the routes.

Let’s examine the current state of the network. On R8 we see that it has learned about R6, but the IIF is null.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVxqNVFG6q5jVRSCSdu4a%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da9c3368b-17c6-41b2-b9b0-ce056d4a7127&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=01c83aeb20327fb24aad00379ab14f24&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FyDFtC0bFEx1jy5L9ls7S%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D06a947e8-6464-4bf4-a092-bce903bc6fad&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ca7945b38a1393d4e83cdd57b723d907&sv=3)

This is because we are running option B, so the PE loopbacks are not leaked between the ASs. R8 cannot perform an RPF check on R6’s loopback.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FY3eRlW73tE3mVOtHagWH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De9e06541-4be6-487c-9762-f791d27e529a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3a4c27fd4f6b262da6400996e81f2642&sv=3)

To fix this, there is a “hack” in PIM in which the ASBR can act as proxy for the PIM Join. R8 uses the BGP nexthop for the type 1 ipv4/mvpn route (10.2.3.2) as the PIM proxy vector. R2 finds the true root of the tree as 10.0.0.6 and builds the tree the rest of the way to R6. To enable this, we use the following command on the PE.

R8 now uses R2 as the “vector.” Note that R9 is the RPF neighbor. If XR is the RPF neighbor, this won’t work, even if I enable **router pim add ipv4 rpf-vector**. Perhaps it’s a bug. For this reason, the links to the XR routers are shut down.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPTxANF6t6xnhSu0JXrmC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0c3a24cc-9f57-4b1f-9361-f162e388a71c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9faf370a29867cc34987416c749125d7&sv=3)

On R3 we see state for all three (S, G) entries. The entry for R6 points to R2 via the NNI. Note that for this to work properly, we don’t seem to be able to use next-hop-self on R3 for ipv4/mvpn. (We _can_ for vpnv4). R3 instead must redistribute the /32 into the IGP. (This was already set in the init file). The **V** flag means Vector.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4JPplwA2lpMp4RNXwxe2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2f2de1b1-241e-4193-8b23-cc523b9e7108&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a14f8d44e921a10b078ed5d24cde8e2f&sv=3)

If we were using C-PIM in the overlay, we would now see all PEs form a PIM adjacency. However, we are using BGP as the overlay instead.

R1 now joins the SSM group in the two VRFs.

R8 finds that the group has an RPF neighbor of R6. How does R8 know this? Isn’t the route to the source via 10.0.0.3?

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5AMTpyUOwXWcX9riAULX%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4b4d0dd8-7d83-4969-aa75-7f9178a28291&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0d44c65fc2b057d2af1d10e728393495&sv=3)

This is because R6 adds a “connector” attribute to the VPNv4 route. As far as I know, this attribute is only used for inter-AS mVPN for this very purpose. It essentially retains the original nexthop and RD on the route.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAZktmwtv1ZnH8BFTJl25%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D88c411fb-972c-4bf7-8fbc-f09b7f9b0945&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=97a5d7e418a6fcac242ebe7f87fa2068&sv=3)

R8 and R10 signal interest via BGP type 7 routes. They use the RD and ingress PE found from the VPNv4 connector attribute. The RT comes from the VPNv4 route as well (the MVPN VRF extcommunity attribute). The source AS field is used for the PE’s loopback when the route is inter-AS. 167772166 in decimal is 10.0.0.6. (Normally for intra-AS this field is the AS number).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZSQaj9umldqU2XQh1e3q%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd9961180-efe8-44dc-9ce6-756645e7b97b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e07ea2db5f34c0c5a7960c6b273d2feb&sv=3)

This is advertised across the NNI and R6 learns of the best route. (XR14 only reflects the route from R10 due to highest RID, but this doesn’t matter, as only one route needs to be advertised to create the state at R6).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvaQABYfInniO0jyc28I9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6b5ba777-cedb-428f-b929-e2d167c64e4e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=43ff2ceed6e40af6b991f5d00174158c&sv=3)

R6 adds this entry to the VRF MRIB. When R1 pings this group, R6 forwards the traffic down the default MDT, to which both R8 and R10 belong. The “client” in both VRFs responds.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbSi1KHpCo3mbCb3WqWHM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da45475cc-d158-4438-ae9f-b16438b4fc7e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=985e6d7c029879bc2bc7a30c8eaaa589&sv=3)

Summary[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-b-mvpn#b3850d8d-b1d1-4f52-8bbe-16936519f228)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Inter-AS option B mVPN seems to only support P-PIM in the underlay. This is because we need a way to proxy the tree building’s Join message at the ASBR. mLDP does not appear to have this feature. mLDP does have the recursive-fec feature, but this only allows the root’s nexthop to be used to proxy the tree building. This is available in option C. But in option B, we don’t even have a remote PE’s loopback in the RIB at all. Only PIM seems to let us use the BGP nexthop for the type 1 ipv4/mvpn route to proxy the PIM Join process.

For this reason, I don’t believe option B mVPN is often supported. It seems it would be easier to go with option C in order to build inter-AS mLDP trees.

# Non-Optimal Multi-Homed Routing | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/non-optimal-multi-homed-routing.md)
.

Load **vpnv4.non-optimal.routing.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:vpnv4.non-optimal.routing.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:vpnv4.non-optimal.routing.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnP9TNE4IGsHzUI2T2HbV%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D55cf7bdd-e36c-4402-8b50-4bcff9c61733&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8d88c63a0eefde8b9068a8d80e2376bd&sv=3)

R1 and XR2 are located at the same customer site. The intention is for R1 to be used as the prefered exit point for routes to remote MPLS sites, so R1 sets LP to 110 on routes received from R2.

Currently there is asymmetric routing between R1 and XR2. Fix this without using BGP policy, and without removing the **as-override** command on the PEs.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/non-optimal-multi-homed-routing#id-3a5ce8ab-f322-45bd-abcc-67398bae3676)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/non-optimal-multi-homed-routing#id-0ce49586-25bb-404d-b6a5-e21f2b82416a)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

R1 is setting LP=110 on all routes received from R2. This includes prefixes that XR2 is advertising. Therefore, R1 is preferring the eBGP route over the iBGP route. (The iBGP route would normally win due to shorter AS path).

If you are not seeing XR2’s routes via eBGP on R1, this is due to the order that the BGP peering sessions came up. R2 is hiding XR2’s prefixes from R1 because it has a bestpath for XR2’s prefixes via R1 itself. You can do a hard reset on R1 so that it will initially learn the prefixes from both peers, and then will choose R2 due to the higher LP.

One way to prevent this is to simply turn off the as-override command on the PEs. The routers would reject the eBGP routes for loop prevention. However, if there are other sites in this VPN which re-use this same ASN, this might not be a good option.

A better solution is to use the SoO (Site of Origin) feature. This essentially just implements an extcommunity filter on the PEs. Routes received from the CE are tagged with the configured SoO value, and any routes to be advertised to the CEs containing this extcomm value are filtered. This is generally much easier than manually configuring a route-map which matches/sets the extcommunity value. All you need to do is associate a SoO value with the BGP neighbor.

On the PEs, we can see that the received VPNv4 updates now have this SoO extcommunity value:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FYlt7Y6zqpmm7858g9Xr1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfbe60114-5a32-482a-acdd-5fe38e797519&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cf1b3d99a31cc0f6aee0b7ef37ca4e22&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Flw9QyiNZk68JRwu3vdiP%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D14456fe1-85e3-4254-865d-9576e4583c60&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bd15dfaad6cc4a46423ce4261403cb50&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FfI0HoHmQBCZMkAOiwFYM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4ccfd99f-d3b2-4ee1-b520-1be58d19ffba&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1ff26439b98c7f5a1f9054569f18c05e&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F1l6PUYqI36OBs470GS29%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da06c3c9f-37df-4bab-a14f-2605113fa82e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=674099058945fc0fa794c020f9bb6b3a&sv=3)

R2 no longer advertises XR2’s prefixes to R1 because the SoO on the route matches R1’s configured SoO. So R1 only has the iBGP path left in its BGP table.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbscJMIne5GecFZGIa6st%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D41e06e98-8441-42a8-ad43-502e63a286f3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=32a30e0dd0441104aa472f2c3aec8772&sv=3)

Note that this solution prevents the MPLS network from being used as a backup path. If the R1-XR2 iBGP session goes down, the routers will no longer have any reachability with each other. But in the real world, these two routers may be directly (physically) connected, so it may not be realistic to say that these routers would need to use the MPLS WAN as backup.

    RP/0/0/CPU0:XR2#traceroute 1.1.1.1 so lo0
    
     1  10.1.19.1 19 msec  9 msec  9 msec
    
    
    RP/0/0/CPU0:XR2#tracer 2001::1:1:1:1 so lo0
    
     1  2001:10:1:19::1 19 msec 9 msec 0 msec

# VRF to Global Internet Access (IOS-XE) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/vrf-to-global-internet-access-ios-xe.md)
.

Load **vpnv4.inet.access.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:vpnv4.inet.access.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:vpnv4.inet.access.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FCY1ufH5uiR4SUAeqcuv9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D31f2c7d8-a41c-4488-9e23-5f9d75e4b259&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1c64b18b845657e91b8d98a18d3159d3&sv=3)

L3VPN is fully setup, with R7 and R8 as CEs. BGP is established with R1 and XR2 in the default table.

Allow R7 and R8 to have access to the internet via R2.

*   They should both be able to ping 1.1.1.1.
    
*   Do not configure any new IP addresses on R7 or R8.
    
*   Do not leak R7s and R8s IP addresses out to the internet.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/vrf-to-global-internet-access-ios-xe#id-8863c03f-69dc-41ea-b0b9-6e872c8ecfbb)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/vrf-to-global-internet-access-ios-xe#id-96b72da0-bdeb-43e4-b671-067378ea95d3)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The easiest way to provide internet access to a VPN is to run the internet in its own VRF. This allows you to easily use RTs and import policies to provide internet access.

Providing internet access in the global table is not as easy. On IOS-XE, we can point a default route in the VRF to the global table, but we must specify a connected/local nexthop.

We do not have a good way to route the return traffic received in the global table back to the original VRF. The only way I can tell to accomplish this is to use the egress PE NAT feature.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/vrf-to-global-internet-access-ios-xe#id-07db8d60-b326-4849-84b6-105a87cd5ba1)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

R7 and R8 can ping 1.1.1.1

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FL8di2ymEMDAR0IusX8WN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da2f19ce2-327b-4990-9ace-c8dc6ad3ace0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a8513778721ee68022daad0b7417d08e&sv=3)

R2 NATs the source to its interface address. Return traffic is automatically routed back into the VRF via the VRF flag on the NAT entry.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJZGBK1Xo5NIOoEksOBdn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcdaac468-a71d-419e-8888-a299a6d0da9b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b44614c69eaefb1d8e7c2b551626fd68&sv=3)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/vrf-to-global-internet-access-ios-xe#id-96b72da0-bdeb-43e4-b671-067378ea95d3)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/vrf-to-global-internet-access-ios-xe#id-07db8d60-b326-4849-84b6-105a87cd5ba1)
    

Copy

    #R3
    router bgp 100
     add vpnv4
      neighbor 2.2.2.2 activate
      neighbor 2.2.2.2 inherit peer-policy IBGP
    
    #R2
    vrf definition VPN_A
     rd 100:1
     route-target export 100:1
     route-target import 100:1
     !
     address-family ipv4
     exit-address-family
    !
    ip route vrf VPN_A 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.1.2.1 global
    !
    router bgp 100
     add vpnv4
      neighbor 3.3.3.3 activate
     add ipv4 vrf VPN_A
      network 0.0.0.0 mask 0.0.0.0
    !
    ip access-list ext SOURCES
     permit ip host 7.7.7.7 any
     permit ip host 8.8.8.8 any
    !
    ip nat inside source list SOURCES int gi2.12 vrf VPN_A overload
    !
    int gi2.12
     ip nat outside
    int gi2.23
     ip nat inside
    int gi2.24
     ip nat inside

# NAT64 Stateful | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateful.md)
.

Load **nat64.lab1.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:nat64.lab1.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR (XR1 only)
    configure
    load bootflash:nat64.lab1.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5yQW6snXnmkMuid24YsS%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D381602d2-4075-4d09-b2c5-56eb8bb6e039&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ec9b9e75907211a47bfb5a28e55490f5&sv=3)

R1 is an internet subscriber and XR1 is an internet server. Configure NAT64 on R6 so that R1 (IPv6-only) can reach XR1 which is IPv4-only (192.0.2.1).

*   Use 100.1.1.1 as the translated IPv4 address on R6
    
*   Only allow traffic sourced from 2001::/64 to be translated for NAT64
    
*   Use the prefix 64:ff96::/96 for NAT64
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateful#id-25addbd3-b3a4-4d11-805b-fa7a96b6bd63)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateful#id-04675350-9b12-42b8-a0ca-597844088c08)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

NAT64 is an IPv6 transition mechanism which allows an IPv6-only host to communicate with IPv4-only hosts. This allows an IPv6-only client to reach the IPv4 internet.

A well-known prefix of 64:ff9b::/96 has been allocated for NAT64. (In this lab we are asked to use 64:ff96::/96, which was an oversight initially by me, but tests your understanding of using a non-default prefix). The IPv4 address is mapped to this prefix to give the IPv6-only client a IPv6 address to use for the IPv4 host. The NAT64 device maps this IP to IPv4, and then source NATs the IPv6 client to a IPv4 address. With stateful NAT, we use a PAT (overload) to conserve IPv4 address space.

To begin, we enable nat64 on all interfaces that will participate in NAT64. This command goes on the IPv6 interfaces which will receive traffic destined to 64:ff96::/96, as well as the outgoing/incoming IPv4 interface.

Next we configure the NAT rules. This is quite similar to NAT44. We use an ACL to define which sources will match the NAT rule, define the NAT64 stateful prefix, define the NAT64 IPv4 NAT pool, and then define the NAT rule. Note that the IPv4 addresses used in the pool cannot exist on the router itself.

R6 will automatically create a NAT virtual interface (NVI). Static routes for the V4 pool (100.1.1.1/32) and the NAT64 prefix are automatically added as well, and point to the NVI:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXtX2auI7MgPbxpunofAi%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D671d4351-3bf2-4b6e-89a3-a006e2a2a0e8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b4311240eab91cfc7c89d33589fb0794&sv=3)

We can now redistribute static into OSPFv3 in order to advertise 64:ff96::/96 into the IGP. This attracts the NAT64 traffic to R6.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateful#id-4dd2ea33-bd81-4b91-a4a0-54e7e84b1a27)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Normally a DNS64 server would be used to resolve A records to AAAA-synthesized records. But in this lab we can manually map 192.0.2.1 to the NAT64 destination address as follows:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FB6zmy2r9wFRMMVnhQ8oD%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da4379358-2f59-4dbe-be62-b49c0806749c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=137b9017ff474c3c6d85aad511327ca0&sv=3)

Since we are allowing all traffic that is sourced from 2001::/64, we can also ping from another host, for example R2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKug8pN7ZnXn76JxytbGL%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D99e8d512-cfe5-4bb5-a343-892d7ca7bfdf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a07fc5834f3a7e287aa5417f5c91c01a&sv=3)

We can see the stateful NAT entries on R6:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrDnzYm5CNwWIIPn4EhKZ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D681d679e-683c-4a7a-b7af-570251f50f76&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bc7873c1cbd32ab4f334b32b346d056e&sv=3)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateful#id-04675350-9b12-42b8-a0ca-597844088c08)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateful#id-4dd2ea33-bd81-4b91-a4a0-54e7e84b1a27)

    int GigabitEthernet2.46

# Inter-AS Option C w/ RT Rewrite | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-c-w-rt-rewrite.md)
.

Load **inter.as.l3vpn.option.c.rt.rewrite.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:inter.as.l3vpn.option.c.rt.rewrite.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:inter.as.l3vpn.option.c.rt.rewrite.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZKkUgltFdY7HKhQAmvt6%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc7bd2884-e7d4-411f-be69-8cafa7b2a967&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=176fe7e3801037367ca1177ca1cf1ced&sv=3)

Inter-AS option C is already fully setup. However, each SP is using its own RT values, and doesn’t want to have to import the other AS’s RT value on every single PE. Configure RT rewrite so that each PE can keep the same RT policy it has for each VRF.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-c-w-rt-rewrite#a6ed57aa-524c-4431-b50e-408a12365955)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-c-w-rt-rewrite#id-4d1ebd1c-5109-40f8-80fa-b38c3e30444f)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As with inter-AS option B, inter-AS option C requires SPs to coordinate the RT values. This lab asks us to do a rewrite operation so that every PE doesn’t have to import the remote SP’s RT value. In the previous lab we did the rewrite operation on the ASBRs in option B. In this lab, we must do the rewrite operation on the RRs, because the RRs are directly peering over eBGP VPNv4.

The rewrite operation uses the same route-map and RPL as we saw in the previous lab. The only difference is where we apply it. Verification is the same as in the previous option B lab, so we won’t cover it again here.

[PreviousInter-AS Option B w/ RT Rewrite](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-b-w-rt-rewrite)
[NextInter-AS Option A Multi-Homed](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-a-multi-homed)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-c-w-rt-rewrite#a6ed57aa-524c-4431-b50e-408a12365955)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-c-w-rt-rewrite#id-4d1ebd1c-5109-40f8-80fa-b38c3e30444f)
    

Copy

    #R5
    ip extcommunity-list standard VPN_A permit rt 200:1
    ip extcommunity-list standard VPN_B permit rt 200:2
    !
    route-map XR2_INBOUND
     match extcomm VPN_A
     set extcommun rt 100:1
    route-map XR2_INBOUND permit 20
     match extcomm VPN_B
     set extcommun rt 100:2
    !
    router bgp 100
     add vpnv4
      neighbor 20.20.20.20 route-map XR2_INBOUND in
    
    #XR2
    route-policy R5_INBOUND
      if extcommunity rt matches-any (100:1) then
        set extcommunity rt (200:1)
      endif
      if extcommunity rt matches-any (100:2) then
        set extcommunity rt (200:2)
      endif
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 200
     neighbor 5.5.5.5
      add vpnv4 uni
       route-policy R5_INBOUND in

# NAT64 Stateless | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateless.md)
.

Load **nat64.lab1.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:nat64.lab1.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR (XR1 only)
    configure
    load bootflash:nat64.lab1.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4MiHuLXYfcywdi5dl7jo%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2b723e34-86c9-4042-91c7-12cf7ac93d01&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=502c2399293afa63d991e397c5f29522&sv=3)

Configure stateless NAT64 on R6 using the following settings:

*   Traffic sourced from R5 will use 2001:db8:64:64::/96 to embed the IPv4 address that should be used for the source NAT.
    
    *   Use IPv4 prefix 100.1.2.3/32 for R5
        
        *   So traffic sourced from R5 will have a source IPv6 address with prefix 2001:db8:64:64::, and 100.1.2.3 mapped as the remaining bits.
            
        
    
*   R5 will embed the IPv4 destination in the IPv6 destination prefix 2001:db8:100:100::/64
    

Test a ping from R5 to XR1 (192.0.2.1)

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateless#id-9588bbb6-5174-4836-802f-9e7210f0f5b2)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateless#id-77a2b697-99b8-4a7c-bb73-ca86cc913f71)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Stateless NAT64 is not very popular, because 1 IPv4 address is used per IPv6 host. There is no address conservation when using stateless NAT.

In stateless NAT64, we enable NAT64 on the interfaces as usual. Also, on the interface facing the IPv6 host, we configure the stateless v6v4 prefix. This is the prefix that has the source host’s intended IPv4 address embedded within it. In this case, we are using 2001:db8:64:64::/96. Traffic sourced from R5 will be 2001:db8:64:64::6401:203, which has 100.1.2.3 embedded within the prefix.

Next we create a route to 100.1.2.3/32 via R5. This creates a static route in the RIB pointing to the NVI. Incoming traffic destined to 100.1.2.3 will use the stateless prefix configured under Gi1.56 to translate back to IPv6.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F9qOap29U093nr4MWq9Vi%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5e394eb0-16a2-4abb-b730-3189059f7704&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=927c606c736a2df724216d13288a2aca&sv=3)

Finally we set the stateless v6 prefix that will be used to embed v4 destinations. You could use 64:ff96::/96 as before, but in this lab we use a /64 to demonstrate a quirk.

When you use a non-/96 prefix for embedding IPv4 addresses, you must be careful about where you embed the IPv4 address. For a /64, there is an 8 bit padding, so the embedded address starts at bit 72. These rules come from RFC6052.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FInWWV1GkZlSDa8rn1Qhg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc5de067c-51a4-415f-af08-a4eb243b921c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=89094a9943bd371b9500ac637d7eb051&sv=3)

So when we ping XR1 from R5, we use **2001:db8:100:100:00c0:0002:0100:0**.

We do not use <prefix>::c000:201. In that case we get back an administratevly prohibited from R6.

Note that since this is stateless NAT64, there will never be any translations seen under **show nat64 translations**. However, you will see hits for “stateless” under **show nat64 statistics**.

[PreviousNAT64 Stateful w/ Static NAT](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateful-w-static-nat)
[NextMAP-T BR](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/map-t-br)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nat/nat64-stateless#id-77a2b697-99b8-4a7c-bb73-ca86cc913f71)

# NSO API using Python | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nso/nso-api-using-python.md)
.

Load **blank.ssh.enabled.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:blank.ssh.enabled.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:blank.ssh.enabled.cfg
    commit replace

Create a python script that interacts with NSO’s northbound API.

*   The script should create Lo303 on R3 with ip address 30.30.30.30/32
    
*   After creating that loopback, the script should interate through all XE devices and print out each Loopback with its name and IP address.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nso/nso-api-using-python#ed57c6aa-1c45-46a7-bf1e-314253118c94)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Create the following python script on the nso server.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FmJsQaL0y4ZmmdgzutuvT%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db8adbd99-a9bc-4570-91dd-1f10c90e78a1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=86cd90683c4182a97eadc7832e0d2eb7&sv=3)

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nso/nso-api-using-python#id-1cb8dde3-d4d1-808c-8c36-f857515aaeee)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

First, we need to understand how the loopback interface is accessed in modeled config. This is different than the native IOS-XE config. We have two ways we can see this. One is using “ | display xpath” from NSO:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZDMMIam6nQXcbCGYJfiS%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1c37a2e3-0186-4b1b-a3f6-396828a0909e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bade5910c4e2951dde66467f0881e943&sv=3)

Another is by staging the config and displaying in XML before aborting.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKVEx2oCapL2FeE3aU3lf%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De7695855-31cd-4079-af0c-ee643a4869b5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=977ba8ce97003dacae9cc7a77237e5a2&sv=3)

This gives us the modeled data for a loopback interface.

First the script starts with the following line, which means to do a single write transaction. The next line gets us to the root of the NCS config database. When opening a transaction, you must at minimum specify the user (’admin’) and the context (’python’, as opposed to CLI, web UI etc). This just allows NSO to audit where the change came from.

Next, we start specifically at device r3 and create the loopback first. We must use the **create()** method. We can’t just assign a new container/list-element using python logic such as **\[’Loopback’\]\[’300’\] = …**. Instead we need to use **create()** so that NSO can validate the new data against the YANG schema.

However, note that while we need to use **.create()** to create a new list, we can use the python **del** to delete a leaf. This is because deleting information does not need to be validated against a YANG schema.

Finally, we add the attributes of the interface (the address and mask). Once the container is created using **create()**, we can add attributes using standard python logic. Using **t.apply()** applies the config (does a commit) within the transaction that we opened.

Next, we use a single read transaction to iterate through all XE devices and print their loopback information. I use an if statement that checks the NED to determine whether this is XE or XR. We’ll see a better way to iterate over a group in the next lab.

[PreviousNSO Template vs. Template Service](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nso/nso-template-vs.-template-service)
[NextNSO API using Python #2](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nso/nso-api-using-python-2)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nso/nso-api-using-python#ed57c6aa-1c45-46a7-bf1e-314253118c94)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/nso/nso-api-using-python#id-1cb8dde3-d4d1-808c-8c36-f857515aaeee)
    

Copy

    import ncs
    
    with ncs.maapi.single_write_trans('admin', 'python') as t:
        root = ncs.maagic.get_root(t)
        device_cbd = root.devices.device['r3']
        device_cbd.config.ios__interface['Loopback'].create('300')
        device_cbd.config.ios__interface.Loopback['300'].ip.address.primary.address = '3.3.3.3'
        device_cbd.config.ios__interface.Loopback['300'].ip.address.primary.mask = '255.255.255.255'
        t.apply()
    
    
    with ncs.maapi.single_read_trans('admin', 'python') as t:
        root = ncs.maagic.get_root(t)
        devices = root.devices
        for device in devices.device:
            if 'ios-cli' in device.device_type.cli.ned_id:
                for interface in device.config.ios__interface.Loopback:
                    print(f'{device.name} has loopback {interface.name} with IP {interface.ip.address.primary.address}')

# Troubleshoot #3 (OSPF) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-3-ospf.md)
.

Load **vpnv4.intra-as.tshoot3.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:vpnv4.intra-as.tshoot3.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:vpnv4.intra-as.tshoot3.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXMgy4cpt5tiRm1vS6CDv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2a0c56f1-32d0-474d-a0d0-3dc59f29b1d8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7575432cf0c28f4b63fde192e33a7025&sv=3)

All OSPFv2 routes are appearing as E2 on R1 and R2. Explain why, and change this so that the Lo0 prefixes are inter-area and the Lo1 prefixes are E2.

OSPFv3 routes are working as intended though already. Why is this?

Also, are all routes present on the CEs?

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-3-ospf#daf6d766-d4f6-4428-8186-a68cb99a2480)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-3-ospf#id-74b0c779-925d-4e85-b185-fa39b19a4dc6)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

For OSPFv2, IOS-XE defaults to using the process ID for the domain ID. IOS-XR defaults to a null domain ID.

We can see this by looking at the OSPF process and VPN routes:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FqEEE4fNbzfctkEMOCG9t%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3e304e16-22a6-459a-bda3-4cb41585bf52&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bba88e1edde2bd653324b28c18ac83ae&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FmyuGcWjEqtMBYa7S75Jd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc5efcfee-ee83-47b8-9ca1-d8c9c84a306a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=828f3f2b839cabe7d7a2afe20e00c805&sv=3)

XR1 is not inserting a domain ID on VPN routes:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZNEyRmO004XhCp5PofIe%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D40f428f6-9b17-4f98-9c8d-76fad536c33e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=db92761ecddeabaf6cdbb8b92a016c7e&sv=3)

To fix this we can simply add the domain ID to XR1 to match what is auto-generated on R2.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fr4f8LKTp04UpQQLsCpu9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcf21b356-8ebb-4b9c-bfb0-82a0d8eb057b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8b400289313e12f10c2ba3a4703e6022&sv=3)

With the domain IDs matching on both sides, both PEs redistribute the BGP routes into OSPF as IA if they came from BGP as type 1, 2 or 3. (This is known via the OSPF route type extcommunity).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FlKFXqe9ZA8YHp6XCsx5x%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da4a275b4-fec2-4650-a248-908d696ffb26&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2344aad7085ae5f805132f40d473a4df&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnUxPbPFEYKx5kQpHEZ8Q%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc5c0ba96-c9ed-4393-bb48-854c70792b85&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a5a08cfc20d11b4942b62e4270cc6034&sv=3)

Notice above that XR2 is missing the E2 route for 10.1.1.1/32. This is because when you redistribute OSPF into BGP on IOS-XE, the external routes are not matched by default.

Now we have the E2 route on XR2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FkmXZFeyJtIiWPFxNMl5o%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd17cb0a4-89b1-4426-8728-3325d1e43a90&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=410eb3fe2b197236014dc7dafcb6992a&sv=3)

### OSPFv3[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-3-ospf#id-4c35735e-cb68-499a-9e16-114a61fa3b2c)

By default for both IOS-XE and IOS-XR, the domain ID is null. IOS-XE does not use the OSPFv3 process ID for the domain ID. Both PEs consider the domain ID to therefore be matching (since both are “null”) so routes appear as IA and E2 as desired by default. The danger with this however, is that by default, other sites that are not supposed to be the same domain, will be by default. So in practice, you likely want to manually define the domain ID value.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FME4DBxsnXF8SEMKRRnWM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9a45fa30-b8ce-431f-9200-205093547fb3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e7b11b36ee24bff62d5c651dd7be8635&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJ3cxuqTn5ttbWEx0K2R0%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D18408973-2ce0-47c6-b638-8a692a4e34b2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=461331d817fdf86ddd5a73b056321b15&sv=3)

The only issue is that IOS-XE is again not redistributing external routes.

# Basic Dial-In using gNMI | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/basic-dial-in-using-gnmi.md)
.

On the ubuntu server (10.200.255.4), bring down the TIG stack using **sudo docker compose down**.

Edit the docker-compose file so that dial\_in is used. Comment out dial\_out.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FDCRk0oPbufZWC7YajzfC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D97f260e1-e314-44d2-94cd-b2009efb52e3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2f4ebddcd2860b2fe3ba0e821e5ae0ba&sv=3)

In NSO, edit the **telegraf\_dial\_in.conf** file and scroll down to “INPUT PLUGINS.” Change the addresses and username/password credentials:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FyZ96dQg8jLcEAoX0VTMG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dad193ced-5831-40b7-b7b4-5ebf080e2466&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9ff5a9a2d5d7d5ed238a232fcfd44db7&sv=3)

Launch the docker container using:

Configure Dial-In MDT on XR1 using the following parameters:

*   Use port 57400
    
*   Do not use TLS
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/basic-dial-in-using-gnmi#id-32a16537-d5e2-4f36-9da3-4400d7017583)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/basic-dial-in-using-gnmi#id-691bbc69-5f55-4393-9f2e-e9e989509513)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MDT using dial-in session initiation is very simple to configure on IOS-XR. You can only use gRPC for dial-in, so all you do is start the gRPC server, set the port, and configure TLS settings. In this lab, we are not using TLS, so we simply use the **no-tls** keyword.

All of the complexity is present on the TIG container. This container is already configured with the YANG model path information.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTFvZFEZvD2KGMLXtLU43%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D42a62cef-7936-4449-b620-bd7469947f17&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=59585c139db2ce4a2f8aced6326fc6e7&sv=3)

On IOS-XR, we can confirm that the session is up:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2umaJKEzvjz69SDkr8iC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc17cea2b-7d07-439b-b453-1103dd8d1c37&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=40b0ad1c3817790bc0c0d3a8b68e368c&sv=3)

Above we see that the destination is dialin. Due to this, the group ID and subscription ID appear to be dynamically generated. The IDs beginning with **GNMI\_\_ refers** to the fact that gNMI is used for the dialin session.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJ8dBa5o88x45FW3fGRbd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8ea48c3d-14bc-4f95-b158-78442baf8a48&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2fd194e74d2bea5b472a19c1a24c0e70&sv=3)

We can also see that the sensor paths were dynamically created. We can tell because the group ID begins with **GNMI\_\_**

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FRkLYU7vJm0MtNbHZL6wZ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2ff276ca-38fe-406c-a2f2-f3e59fbb87ee&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5dec8d330795bd88906fbcabf27340f5&sv=3)

We should also be aware of the commands to view more general gRPC status. The following command shows that the gRPC server is running, TLS is disabled, and the router is listening on port 57400.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FmFZ12ydNXjdQYeOgcShr%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6bdde478-7afc-4367-8037-4b512ec56fc5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=241e73aeaf585cb1e8846d93e859d66b&sv=3)

We can also see the current gRPC streams:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FQMr6DjNbWyIKCzXFtsFx%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd6dc3be4-cdef-4117-8cce-e76b7972941d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=dc18ed1a1cf5e70c035618894c1cffc3&sv=3)

Interestingly, the gRPC statistics shows all counters as zero. All of these appear to be actions such as replace/delete config, get operational data, etc.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5QhRqHpWOFCILDlCYJWx%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De162d5a6-7bf0-4d3f-ac5f-a95c09aaeb64&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=061611a6d5db3701dcded8fe3d9ce1df&sv=3)

About gNMI[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/basic-dial-in-using-gnmi#f10e74cf-131b-4af6-8511-39b82af1426f)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

gNMI stands for gRPC Network Management Interface. This is a network management protocol that is yang-based, very much like NETCONF. Where NETCONF uses SSH for transport, gNMI uses gRPC (which itself uses HTTP2, which allows for TLS). Where NETCONF uses XML for encoding, gNMI uses proto buffs. This allows for compressed data, giving gNMI better throughput and scalability than NETCONF.

gNMI uses four functions:

*   Capabilities
    
*   Get
    
*   Set
    
*   Subscribe
    

The subscribe function is what we are interested in for MDT. The collector initiates (dials in) the session with the router, and using the subscribe function, specifies the YANG model, encoding type, and streaming interval (i.e. 30seconds). This is why we don’t have to configure any of these parameters on the router itself.

You may have seen that IOS-XR has recently begun supporting gNMI for dialout as well. How can that work? The way it works is that the router initiates a session with the collector using the **grpc tunnel** command. This appears to just allow the collector to learn about the router. Then the collector initiates the MDT session by using the subscribe function like normal. So gNMI still works the same as always. The difference is just that the router can inform the collector of its presence, allowing the collector to send the subscribe message and start the MDT session.

# Finding the correct YANG model #2 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/finding-the-correct-yang-model-2.md)
.

Configure MDT using the solution from the first lab:

Copy

    #XR1
    telemetry model-driven
     destination-group TIG
      address-family ipv4 10.100.100.1 port 57500
       encoding self-describing-gpb
       protocol grpc no-tls
      !
     !
     sensor-group SENSOR1
      sensor-path Cisco-IOS-XR-infra-statsd-oper:infra-statistics/interfaces/interface/latest/generic-counters
     !
     subscription SUB1
      sensor-group-id SENSOR1 sample-interval 5000
      destination-id TIG

Configure a static delay value for Gi0/0/0/0.12 under performance-measurement. Add an additional sensor-path which exports the performance measurement delay for only this interface.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/finding-the-correct-yang-model-2#id-51219ff0-d610-4536-af7d-245172f02196)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/finding-the-correct-yang-model-2#id-23f228ac-5d2b-43c9-9799-a4af68b1598f)

This path is a bit easier to find. First I use **yang-operational** to find the YANG model that contains the show output for performance-measurement:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FqQi5zsWGiB76JCEJSUnJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df6c2462a-b251-4933-ba1a-f8501467105e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=fbbf48cd378ae3a880c5e2d6b9f382cb&sv=3)

        r._measurement == "Cisco-IOS-XR-perf-meas-oper:performance-measurement/nodes/node/interfaces/interface-details/interface-detail" and

# Option A L2NNI | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-a-l2nni.md)
.

Load **russo.pl.course.inter-as.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure inter-AS option A support for an L2NNI between R2 and R3. CSR1 should have connectivity on VRF L2A and VRF L2B. An OSPF adjacency will form once connectivity is established.

*   Use EVPN E-LAN in Globomantics (R6 to R2)
    
*   Use EVPN-VPWS in Wired Brain (R8 to R3)
    
*   BGP l2vpn/evpn is already enabled in both ASs
    
*   Use Q-in-Q 3999/168 on R6 to R1, and Q-in-Q 3998/268 on R8 to R1
    
*   Use VLAN 1000 on the R2-R3 link
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-a-l2nni#id-2a9189ae-7450-402a-bc19-9412ecb7c077)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-a-l2nni#id-6f03271b-060c-4bf0-ad07-80fe43ee0b57)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In option A inter-AS for L3VPN, ASBRs do back-to-back VRF, treating each other as CEs. We can say that option A inter-AS for L2VPN is the same thing, in which the ASBRs treat each other as L2 CEs. Each provider can use its own L2VPN technology, as demonstrated in this lab. The drawback is that one VLAN is needed per L2VPN, and MAC address learning must occur on each ASBR.

First we setup E-LAN EVPN in AS65001. We see that R6 and R2 each advertise the MACs learned on the CE link. R2 treats the ASBR link as a CE link, performing MAC address learning.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FiI4dsGzHGutm0zzRHoQs%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D182e928c-bbd7-4703-971a-20d24ce60947&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2e23adf52dcb5a9d916bb02d7f3bb76f&sv=3)

R6 knows the local CE’s MAC via the EFP, and the remote CE’s MAC via R2.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FqjvJRm1VaozTJG29rB2a%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc9b023b2-3a4b-4d37-bcc7-590afe866fc3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=19660e0680c8f136695b3f6120cf56eb&sv=3)

AS65002 uses EVPN-VPWS instead. In this case, R3 does not do any MAC learning, simply transporting received frames to the Z end. We see that R3 and R8 only advertise AD routes:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FfldUXz3SfUR1UWeUYBjc%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D54afeedc-a1e3-45cc-9145-e538dc12cdaf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=54b1324619eff6a628bc4d2819c7a347&sv=3)

On R3, the EVPN-VPWS VC is up:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FYOU847y6VBs4LrXAFnYR%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D814e9103-c98d-4a0a-a4a5-76c9de58ff1e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3f6dbea2c2e34873bb5b3a0c96e11ace&sv=3)

R1 has OSPF adjacencies between its two L2 VRFs, L2A and L2B:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FqZVsDUiJpUp07gFnZIvF%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D15f868ff-0178-4730-8fdf-a6acdd572e09&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=09186bc76ffd4f105e79a5e103fe86e1&sv=3)

Copy

    #R6
    l2vpn evpn
     replication-type ingress
    !
    l2vpn evpn instance 100 vlan-based
    !
    int gi2
     service instance 100 eth
      encapsulation dot1q 3999 second-dot1q 168
      rewrite ingress tag pop 2 symmetric
      exit
     exit
    !
    bridge-domain 100
     member evpn-instance 100
     member gi2 service-instance 100
    
    #R2
    l2vpn evpn
     replication-type ingress
    !
    l2vpn evpn instance 100 vlan-based
    !
    int gi2
     service instance 100 eth
      encapsulation dot1q 1000
      rewrite ingress tag pop 1 symmetric
      exit
     exit
    !
    bridge-domain 100
     member evpn-instance 100
     member gi2 service-instance 100
    
    #R3
    int gi2
     service instance 100 eth
      encapsulation dot1q 1000
      rewrite ingress tag pop 1 symmetric
      exit
     exit
    !
    l2vpn evpn instance 100 point-to-point
     vpws context CUSTOMER
      member gi2 service-instance 100
      service target 100 source 100
    
    #R8
    int gi2
     service instance 100 eth
      encapsulation dot1q 3998 second-dot1q 268
      rewrite ingress tag pop 2 symmetric
      exit
     exit
    !
    l2vpn evpn instance 100 point-to-point
     vpws context CUSTOMER
      member gi2 service-instance 100
      service target 100 source 100

# Partitioned RRs with IOS-XR | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/partitioned-rrs-with-ios-xr.md)
.

Load **vpnv4.partitioned.rr.xr.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:vpnv4.partitioned.rr.xr.init.cfg 
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:vpnv4.partitioned.rr.xr.init.cfg 
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsqnZJquBs8gUFGEhLnMC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D345eb557-83e9-4773-9e04-d5d0faa0a752&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9f1dc0df50e751edadc6479447d8253f&sv=3)

This is the same as the previous lab, except the RR is moved from R6 to XR1. The CE, XR2, is peered with R6 now.

The L3VPN is fully setup. All PEs are peered with the two RRs. Configure R3 to only accept VPN\_A routes and configure XR1 to only accept VPN\_B routes.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/partitioned-rrs-with-ios-xr#cc4b4c35-5077-4d68-9536-e3904c1b754e)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/partitioned-rrs-with-ios-xr#id-2081f1cd-961c-4f1a-9fcc-47378aa74440)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This lab tests your understanding of applying RT filters in IOS-XR.

As a review, in IOS-XE you can disable the RT filter in three ways:

1.  Configuring the VRF locally, and importing the RT
    
2.  Configuring the router as an RR
    
3.  Disabling the RT filter
    

To configure the IOS-XE router as a RR that selectively accepts VPNv4 updates, you use an RR group.

On IOS-XR, the same three methods are available for disabling the default RT filter:

1.  Configure the VRF locally and import the RT
    
2.  Configure the router as an RR
    
3.  Disable the RT filter
    

To selectively import VPNv4 prefixes on an IOS-XR RR, you simply associate a route-policy with the **retain route-target** command.

On XR1, we can see that the only VPNv4 routes in the table are for VPN\_B:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FfA5ofmDttxaaYIZkFewH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2916ccbc-b03e-4526-b88b-c9e5850ac7e3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c67515c20b274ae36dc042e70113a667&sv=3)

If we **debug bgp update** we can see that the VPN\_A routes are denied due to the RT filter:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F8q7G2luWGXlStMs5690r%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D32cd2a88-4cb9-4413-a11a-b0f0bf0ca252&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ba9337ecf41c893657bf62b35bf3932a&sv=3)

[PreviousPartitioned RRs](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/partitioned-rrs)
[NextRT Filter](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/rt-filter)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/partitioned-rrs-with-ios-xr#cc4b4c35-5077-4d68-9536-e3904c1b754e)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/partitioned-rrs-with-ios-xr#id-2081f1cd-961c-4f1a-9fcc-47378aa74440)
    

Copy

    #R3
    ip extcommunity-list standard PERMITTED_VPNv4 permit rt 100:1
    !
    router bgp 100
     template peer-session IBGP
      remote-as 100
      update-so lo0
     exit-peer-session
     !
     template peer-policy IBGP
      route-reflector-client
     exit-peer-policy
     !
     neighbor 2.2.2.2 inherit peer-session IBGP
     neighbor 4.4.4.4 inherit peer-session IBGP
     neighbor 5.5.5.5 inherit peer-session IBGP
     neighbor 6.6.6.6 inherit peer-session IBGP
     !
     add vpnv4
      bgp rr-group PERMITTED_VPNv4
      neighbor 2.2.2.2 activate
      neighbor 2.2.2.2 inherit peer-policy IBGP
      neighbor 4.4.4.4 activate
      neighbor 4.4.4.4 inherit peer-policy IBGP
      neighbor 5.5.5.5 activate
      neighbor 5.5.5.5 inherit peer-policy IBGP
      neighbor 6.6.6.6 activate
      neighbor 6.6.6.6 inherit peer-policy IBGP
    
    #XR1
    route-policy VPNv4_RETAIN
      if extcommunity rt matches-any (100:2) then
        pass
      endif
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 100
     address-family ipv4 unicast
     !
     address-family vpnv4 unicast
      retain route-target route-policy VPNv4_RETAIN
     !
     neighbor-group IBGP
      remote-as 100
      update-source Loopback0
      address-family vpnv4 unicast
       route-reflector-client
     !
     neighbor 2.2.2.2
      use neighbor-group IBGP
     !
     neighbor 4.4.4.4
      use neighbor-group IBGP
     !
     neighbor 5.5.5.5
      use neighbor-group IBGP
     !
     neighbor 6.6.6.6
      use neighbor-group IBGP

Copy

    router bgp 100
     no bgp default route-target filter

Copy

    ip extcommunity-list standard PERMITTED_VPNv4 permit rt 100:1
    !
    router bgp 100
     add vpnv4
      bgp rr-group PERMITTED_VPNv4

Copy

    router bgp 100
     add vpnv4 uni
      retain route-target all

Copy

    route-policy VPNv4_RETAIN
      if extcommunity rt matches-any (100:2) then
        pass
      endif
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 100
     address-family vpnv4 unicast
      retain route-target route-policy VPNv4_RETAIN
