# Troubleshoot #4 (OSPF Inter-AS) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-4-ospf-inter-as.md)
.

Load **vpnv4.inter-as.tshoot4.init.cfg.** On R2, you may need to replace with **blank.cfg** first.

Copy

    #IOS-XE (R1-R4, R7-R10)
    config replace flash:vpnv4.inter-as.tshoot4.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:vpnv4.inter-as.tshoot4.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FtIp5hni11jpNQDT72X5T%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd6a0bc5a-e967-4230-8fb8-bf37808f37e3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4dda854f067f27caed27a176942038c6&sv=3)

The PE-CE protocol for both VPNs is OSPF. Currently there is no reachability between sites located in opposite ASs. Explain the issue and find a way to fix it.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-4-ospf-inter-as#id-448111e1-1fb6-4514-b044-c6d9b0b0cbaa)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-4-ospf-inter-as#dda1d57a-9b59-47f4-af69-96dee4c70911)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, when running OSPF in a VRF on a CE device, the OSPF process will not install any routes learned from LSAs with the down bit set. This is a loop prevention mechanism. The assumption is that if the device is running OSPF in a VRF, then it must be a PE, in which case it should reject OSPF routes that came from the MPLS core so that they have no chance of being redistributed back into BGP.

However, in option A, the ASBRs essentially act as CE devices. So we need to disable this check to allow the ASBRs to install the OSPF routes into the VRF RIB.

On R1 we can see than LSAs injected by XR1 have the down bit set. This indicates that the route was redistributed from BGP VPNv4/6 into OSPF, so any other PEs that learn this LSA should not redistribute these routes _back_ into BGP.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FUmGesyNyqLpQrqJzTQEn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2b0f69c2-2106-49dd-9dae-337f28229b32&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8c5edbc26a8e0ae7fc7e4f25a02f585b&sv=3)

Due to this, the router will not install 10.10.10.10/32 into the VRF RIB. However, if there were any other downstream OSPF neighbors in this VRF on R1 which did not run OSPF in a VRF, those routers could actually install the 10.10.10.10/32 route. This is because the LSAs must be flooded throughout the area, and those other routers wouldn’t care about the downward bit. However, traffic would be blackholed at R1. You can essentially think of this feature as a distribute-list filter, which filters LSAs with the down bit from being entered into the VRF RIB locally.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FgzZQyK1dcS5BIRcDCYK0%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df62e951d-adf6-459c-b204-e18146d5a693&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7159e1d7c19da135ddaa2894c54f9a3f&sv=3)

We turn off this check using **capability vrf-lite**. This command is meant for routers that are running VRF lite (using VRF functionality simply for separation of routing tables, without using MPLS VPNv4/v6).

The LSA from XR1 is unchanged, but R1 no longer filters the routes from the VRF RIB.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFq7JRqbPgzi99FqGITTq%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2775fca0-8d4d-4fda-bf1c-972f080da0ed&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7db0eb5d9db305545929e326fa4f5bc4&sv=3)

Interestingly, this is enough to get traffic to work. Since R1 is no longer a “PE”, it is redistributing BGP routes into OSPF as external without the down bit set now. Notice below that the down bit is not set. The route tag encodes AS 100, which also passes XR1’s check (because it is in BGP ASN 200 not 100).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FN2ETh4sKOvLVUFibKE52%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8ab984cc-9b02-4dd0-9ad0-4213d6bb49b4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f06e76e555a44837877792837ebf1bf1&sv=3)

So now XR1 can install this in the RIB.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FpT79qNcHidyAqb8kG8Io%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5f94674f-452e-4f1f-b50b-0940fabd46cc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=96f0efc1ef1feb0c8002fe4d403152f7&sv=3)

Traffic is working end-to-end:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPIUqM2p0IVNgRnqWetUg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd5230ffb-efac-488f-bba5-0f8af732c4e7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=214db79cf9a283e00945d7fac9e8df25&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F8s2PdHnxcG0t5Vh2QMuU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D92c9ae4c-1cc4-499b-a9f6-14ac6352e7a6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=97064a67219e185f49cb56f6eca2a98c&sv=3)

Notice that on the AS100 side, the routes are showing up as O IA. This is because XR1 is still a “true” PE, and is redistributing the AS200 routes as inter-area. R1, even though it is running **capability vrf-lite**, still encodes the OSPF domain ID and route-type into the BGPv4 route. This allows R2 to redistribute the routes as inter-area to the CEs.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2U151G6TTV1IIMhWXbl9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3af13192-3d4b-4a4a-81d8-65cf8690f3c3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6e515f85992a5b79da9975ef80e80388&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fq3oC1HC3g1lQsBir5b6y%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D01607684-18c1-47be-8d0f-a08c19a03540&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=481b401dddebce725437251c161d424f&sv=3)

On the AS200 side, R1 is now redistributing routes into OSPF as E2, because it is not a “true” PE. It acts more like CE when redistributing from BGP into OSPF. So AS200 must keep these as external, even though the domain ID technically matches (which is null by default on IOS-XR).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVeGvWuWpMYsNeUHAL1pN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7a87501f-dfa9-4619-b32b-35db134e95e8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6a3b165b0c33402efa60c7790ba61ba0&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F7B6ANMvuqbIpm3T5DtmY%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Daabf7fd6-efd8-423b-97d1-35832eb2ff74&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4d55cfb86457e5cf24d92199a68693b3&sv=3)

Even though it is not required, we should tell XR1 to ignore the down bit as well. AS200 doesn’t want to rely on AS100 setting **capability vrf-lite** on their side. On XR1, if we set **capability vrf-lite**, we break reachability. This is because on IOS-XE, external OSPF routes are not redistributed into BGP by default. XR1 now has the same behavior as R1 - it redistributes the routes as external instead of inter-area. Instead of fixing this on R1, let’s use a different method, which simply tells XR1 to continue to act as a true PE but ignore the down bit on LSAs.

At this point nothing has changed, because R1 is not setting the down bit anyways. XR1 is still redistributing routes as inter-area. However, if we remove capability VRF-lite on R1, XR1 will now ignore the down bit and still install these routes in its VRF RIB.

R1 now redistributes routes as inter-area again, and sets the down bit.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fs68wu498OTuVBbaqFBGZ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D994d932a-8a51-4884-9bcc-b37e3825f8ee&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=83578b477fd151fd9e418363bbd60815&sv=3)

XR1 ignores the down bit, and the CEs in AS200 will see the route as inter-area.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FdTaTAYykgZZnNqUoLPQB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D416e390c-78f5-4e1c-af1c-547a239218a0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b10567ee65e4d4734c46f5c4640a07c2&sv=3)

Summary[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-4-ospf-inter-as#id-1bc8dde3-d4d1-8099-930b-f5eec8ce9325)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

IOS-XE only has one knob: **capability vrf-lite**. This causes the router to ignore the down bit, but also ignore the OSPF domain ID/route type when redistributing BGP VPNv4 routes into OSPF. All routes become E2 routes.

On IOS-XR, we have two knobs: **capability vrf-lite** and **disable-dn-bit-check**. The **capability vrf-lite** knob acts like IOS-XE. BGP routes are always redistributed into OSPF as E2. However, the **disable-dn-bit-check** knob retains the inter-area redistribution functionality (when domain ID matches and route-type is intra/inter-area), but still allows the router to install LSAs with the DN bit set into the VRF RIB.

[PreviousTroubleshoot #3 (OSPF)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-3-ospf)
[NextVRF to Global Internet Access (IOS-XE)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/vrf-to-global-internet-access-ios-xe)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-4-ospf-inter-as#id-448111e1-1fb6-4514-b044-c6d9b0b0cbaa)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-4-ospf-inter-as#dda1d57a-9b59-47f4-af69-96dee4c70911)
    
*   [Summary](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/intra-as-l3vpn/troubleshoot-4-ospf-inter-as#id-1bc8dde3-d4d1-8099-930b-f5eec8ce9325)
    

Copy

    #R1
    router ospf 1 vrf VPN_A
     capability vrf-lite
    router ospf 2 vrf VPN_B
     capability vrf-lite
    
    #XR1
    router ospf 1 vrf VPN_A
     disable-dn-bit-check
    router ospf 2 vrf VPN_B
     disable-dn-bit-check

Copy

    #R1
    router ospf 1
     capability vrf-lite
    router ospf 2
     capability vrf-lite

Copy

    #XR1
    router ospf 1
     vrf VPN_A
      disable-dn-bit-check
    !
    router ospf 2
     vrf VPN_B
      disable-dn-bit-check

Copy

    #R1
    router ospf 1
     no capability vrf-lite

# Dial-Out with TLS | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/dial-out-with-tls.md)
.

Within NSO, edit the **telegraf\_dial\_out.conf** file. Uncomment the TLS lines under INPUT PLUGINS:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fufx6XYfcwfau3PfiE1AI%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df03d88e3-f319-47ac-a526-ac3be37e409c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=46651011b0e9ae0b6cd92abfc8dcc0f6&sv=3)

Follow these steps to create certificates for the server: [https://xrdocs.io/telemetry/tutorials/telemetry-stack-update-grpc-tls/#telegraf-certificate](https://xrdocs.io/telemetry/tutorials/telemetry-stack-update-grpc-tls/#telegraf-certificate)

Note that I had to do this after following all of those steps:

Edit the **docker-compose.yaml** file. Add the three lines to copy the cert files to the container. Set the method to dial\_out.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fn6w323DgkQaoOq8QhARq%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dbd7c4715-312a-4230-aaeb-ea3d98cde8d7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=09be99c15e5e86381ab97b512e24b2cd&sv=3)

Stop and then launch the container

Configure Dial-Out MDT on XR1 using the following parameters:

*   The collector is 10.10.40.17:57500
    
*   Use GPB-KV
    
*   Use gRPC using TLS
    
    *   SCP the root CA cert to the router using `scp CA.pem clab@10.100.100.101:/harddisk:/` within Ubuntu. This file is located in the /tig-stack-qos-interface-statistics directory.
        
    *   Place the CA.pem file in the correct directory on the router using **run cp /harddisk\\:/CA.pem …**
        
        *   You will have to figure out the destination location on your own!
            
        
    *   Restart the EMSD process using: `process restart emsd`
        
    *   Use the tls-hostname `telegraf.lab` for the server
        
    
*   Use the YANG model **Cisco-IOS-XR-infra-statsd-oper:infra-statistics/interfaces/interface/latest/generic-counters**
    
*   Push the data at a 5 second interval to the collector
    

Login to Grafana at http://10.200.255.4 using admin/admin123. Use the following grafana query to confirm the MDT is working:

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/dial-out-with-tls#id-485c3631-cb9d-4943-854a-9f072d4721d9)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mdt/dial-out-with-tls#id-7ab57d2a-59f8-4944-b03d-f2e4c4114410)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When using dial out MDT, the router is the client and the collector is the server. (The router initiates the TCP connection with the collector). The collector sends its certificate to the server to authenticate itself. The router needs the public cert of the root CA to verify the collector’s cert.

This means that we need to copy the root CA to the router. We do this using SCP from the Ubuntu node.

Next, we need to copy the file to the correct location on the router. The router only looks for the cert in /misc/config/grpc/dialout/dialout.pem. The filename is important - it must match exactly. We use the bash cp command to copy the file to this location.

Now that the root CA is present, we just configure dial out MDT as usual, but set the TLS parameters. We just need to specify the TLS hostname that is present in the cert the server is sending, which in this case is **telegraf.lab**. (The cert was generated with this hostname).

Traffic should now be working. You should see data in Grafana using the below query.

We can see in a pcap that traffic is correctly encrypted using TLSv1.3:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FUa5LuYHDqs84DRnkYAn1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Daa2b6507-8039-46dd-b3a4-c88ff62f2331&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e9a975df769dc0ca5e6be7ad7f9c6b00&sv=3)

We can also see on the router that the connection is using grpc with TLS:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FQXVxiAfU65zjLktwTW8a%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D439f9d20-dd9b-4206-bf9a-56efb89457ee&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=92f8d6330173605cf1275e3dbb6f4d85&sv=3)

If the session is not connecting, we can use the command **show telemetry model-driven trace go-info | in TLS** to help troubleshot. Below is the message you would see when there is no cert present in /misc/config/grpc/dialout/dialout.pem

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FlT5CSV6JwVVgHmzZgH6Z%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3992ad2d-51d0-4955-9250-83e69a55fe77&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=45151efa213b90a9c6be68b83b4c8a5f&sv=3)

When it is working, you will see a message similar to this:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAhGdEYnqU1z72gbzeVbf%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcc00f385-6a43-412b-a861-1bd5b6b6db47&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=69c1705b53d8bd68f5f8cd8d0c5369df&sv=3)

Note that gRPC is required for using TLS. While TCP is a valid transport method for Dial Out, it cannot be used with TLS.

# RPKI on IOS-XE (Enabling the feature) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/bgp-rpki/rpki-on-ios-xe-enabling-the-feature.md)
.

Load **ios-xe.rpki.enable.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE (R1, R2, R3)
    config replace flash:ios-xe.rpki.enable.init.cfg

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAwSkudfYFKh26RYUFiae%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D530aba5f-42ca-4c23-9b09-590048b04f76&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5a881a6184825bfa54432fbc283b33fe&sv=3)

BGP is already setup between R1-R2 and R2-R3.

Configure RPKI on R2 for both IPv4 and IPv6, but do not use the information for local policy yet. We only want R2 to connect to the RPKI server and we want to see that R2 is loading the ROAs correctly, but we don’t want R2 to act on this information yet and actually perform any validity checks.

The RPKI server is reachable at 10.100.100.1 on port 3323.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/bgp-rpki/rpki-on-ios-xe-enabling-the-feature#d1240d53-b4b3-4447-9a00-a892f1d2cbd7)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/bgp-rpki/rpki-on-ios-xe-enabling-the-feature#id-0f2740c6-e149-4a2a-bfa5-8a05914ae3f2)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

BGP RPKI Route Origination Validation is a BGP security mechanism which reduces malicious and accidental route origination from the wrong AS. This prevents incidents such as the YouTube hijacking of 2008. During this incident, an AS attempted to null route YouTube’s prefix, but accidentally leaked Youtube’s prefix out to the internet, breaking YouTube’s traffic.

In RPKI Route Origination, each AS issues ROAs (Route Origination Authorizations) with the RIR. Typically the RIR hosts the signed ROAs, but each AS has the option to host their own CA and sign ROAs if they want. Each ROA object has three pieces of information:

*   The prefix (i.e. 1.0.0.0/22)
    
*   The max prefix length (i.e. /24)
    
*   The originating AS (i.e. 14003)
    

The ROA is a certification that the prefix can be announced by the originating AS. Announcements from other originating ASs should not be trusted.

The RIR signs this ROA and adds it to the RPKI repository. A route validation server, such as Routinator in our lab, is needed to load all ROAs from all RIRs, and interface with the routers. The routers use the RtR (RPKI to Router) protocol to pull in the database of ROAs from Routinator. The routers then use this locally to determine whether a given prefix:

*   Is valid (the prefix, prefix len, and originating AS match an ROA)
    
*   Is invalid (the prefix and prefix len match an ROA, but the originating AS is different)
    
*   Is not found (the prefix and prefix len do not match any ROA)
    

Note that this system does not validate the entire AS path. Only the originating AS (the first AS in the path) is validated using this system. This is “route origination validation” and not “path validation.”

### Enabling RPKI on IOS-XE[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/bgp-rpki/rpki-on-ios-xe-enabling-the-feature#d306a660-4a45-4c9c-b1bc-15632149caa8)

On IOS-XE, we can only use TCP to interface with the RPKI server. This command enables the TCP connection:

Upon establishing the connection, the router will automatically start downloading ROAs and using them for prefix validation. The router will reject any prefixes that are invalid (they have a matching ROA but the originating AS is not valid).

To prevent this, and simply establish the connection without “doing anything” with the RPKI information, we use the following command:

This is different from the similar command **bgp bestpath prefix-validate allow-invalid**, which allows invalid prefixes to still be accepted and used as a bestpath. However, with the **allow-invalid** command, prefix validation is still occuring, and a valid prefix will be preferred over an invalid prefix. IOS inserts this validity check before the local preference in the bestpath algorithm. So to fully disable this behavior, we use the **disable** keyword instead of **allow-invalid**.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/bgp-rpki/rpki-on-ios-xe-enabling-the-feature#id-97716daa-ffb1-4562-894e-c8a562ec542b)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Notice that the BGP table has RPKI validation codes.

*   **V** means the prefix has a matching ROA
    
*   **I** means the prefix has an ROA but the originating AS is not valid
    
*   **N** means the prefix does not have a matching ROA, so the validity cannot be verified
    

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMjy0E1eKwpcfItRyH2rC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D892f2998-10fa-4970-bda8-0c6b085ea1e9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4f900b61322e6696f07b19a767c92c84&sv=3)

Because we have disabled prefix validation for IPv4/uni and IPv6/uni, we should not see these codes in our BGP tables:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsZxjZgfTeKkRGOX6tNT9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D186476a2-117c-47d8-bc95-f3468507f434&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1c7564d6584fcd7ea4dd3b3a46ec4066&sv=3)

However, we should be able to see status about the RPKI server and browse the RPKI table. We can see information about the TCP connection using the following command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvGXn93YKgq7N5hk7mnIl%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4aebf4ae-8a15-4182-b50c-7a9661252bc1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b6e48cc5558e6f93acc8467d3f71e6a5&sv=3)

More importantly, we can browse the RPKI table for both IPv4 and IPv6:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsX9FwdevcAiHior4ydkL%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df0493971-eb72-4051-b71f-5800138be8d0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=49c1eeba7b702dabb728faeacf6c41df&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fvuv0JnmHz0Onl2UExksK%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df9ba4c84-eea4-4ed2-8731-d773df174588&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7b206c5fc3e4acbdd904bb4466a26b4d&sv=3)

The table is fairly self explanatory. The **maxlen** column works sort of like **le** in a prefix list. For example, look at 1.6.8.0/22. The maxlen is 24, so the prefixes 1.6.8.0/22, 1.6.8.0/23, 1.6.9.0/24, etc, will match this ROA.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPF20azT1qoC1KpOPlOsu%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D72a8c0a3-2811-40a6-98d1-9b658a508e0e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8007eaa9bc332c2ce2aef72153dc2d94&sv=3)

In the next lab we will begin acting on this information.

# Inter-AS Option B w/ RT Rewrite | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-b-w-rt-rewrite.md)
.

Load **inter.as.l3vpn.option.b.rt.rewrite.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:inter.as.l3vpn.option.b.rt.rewrite.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:inter.as.l3vpn.option.b.rt.rewrite.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FBWl1vDQEzE4fgh3OT3lt%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D38d1bcc4-b906-4662-a375-91138f275e50&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=018e3e71cdbdf086bfc7e850a717ab89&sv=3)

Option B is already fully setup. But the SPs do not want to import each other’s RT values on every single PE. Currently the inter-AS L3VPN traffic is not working because of this. Use RT rewrite on the ASBRs to fix this.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-b-w-rt-rewrite#b6efadc9-02f6-49fc-b713-906ebc496720)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation/Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-b-w-rt-rewrite#id-4a6b1ec9-003b-4f07-ba7e-08719f6336d2)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Inter-AS option B requires coordination of RT values between the SPs. In this lab, the SPs do not want to have to import the other SP’s RT value on every single VRF of every PE. Instead, we are asked to configure an RT rewrite policy on the ASBRs.

On R1, we identify the two RT values that AS200 uses for VPN\_A and VPN\_B. We then set this to our own RT value for these VPNs. This is applied to the neighbor XR1 inbound.

On R2, we now see that remote VPNv4 updates have the RT of 100:1 instead of 200:1. This allows R2 to import the routes without any changes on R2 itself.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FfTaJsDc5bu9gRM7GGm46%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db2d82ea0-6f5f-4d71-b370-4c8c281fa05e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=75899a9620e1070c5ba6744e76a34a6c&sv=3)

We do the same on XR1, matching the remote AS’s RT values and translating these to AS200’s RT value.

This allows XR2 to import the VPNv4 routes without any changes.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FW5Bk28RZkpbvXUudZv52%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6271b56e-8d9f-4fe8-b81b-9001a3410cb4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8dddfc641f76cf84023ae3fbd98a3239&sv=3)

Note that there was no need to alter the RD values, as these are just used to keep VPNv4 updates separated in the global VPNv4 table.

[PreviousInter-AS Option C - iBGP LU](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-c-ibgp-lu)
[NextInter-AS Option C w/ RT Rewrite](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-c-w-rt-rewrite)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-b-w-rt-rewrite#b6efadc9-02f6-49fc-b713-906ebc496720)
    
*   [Explanation/Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/inter-as-option-b-w-rt-rewrite#id-4a6b1ec9-003b-4f07-ba7e-08719f6336d2)
    

Copy

    #R1
    ip extcommunity-list standard VPN_A permit rt 200:1
    ip extcommunity-list standard VPN_B permit rt 200:2
    !
    route-map XR1_INBOUND
     match extcommunity VPN_A
     set extcommunity rt 100:1
    route-map XR1_INBOUND permit 20
     match extcommunity VPN_B
     set extcommunity rt 100:2
    !
    router bgp 100
     add vpnv4
      neighbor 30.1.19.19 route-map XR1_INBOUND in
    
    #XR1
    route-policy R1_INBOUND
      if extcommunity rt matches-any (100:1) then
        set extcommunity rt (200:1)
      endif
      if extcommunity rt matches-any (100:2) then
        set extcommunity rt (200:2)
      endif
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 200
     neighbor 30.1.19.1
      add vpnv4 uni
       route-policy R1_INBOUND in

Copy

    #R1
    ip extcommunity-list standard VPN_A permit rt 200:1
    ip extcommunity-list standard VPN_B permit rt 200:2
    !
    route-map XR1_INBOUND
     match extcommunity VPN_A
     set extcommunity rt 100:1
    route-map XR1_INBOUND permit 20
     match extcommunity VPN_B
     set extcommunity rt 100:2
    !
    router bgp 100
     add vpnv4
      neighbor 30.1.19.19 route-map XR1_INBOUND in

Copy

    #XR1
    route-policy R1_INBOUND
      if extcommunity rt matches-any (100:1) then
        set extcommunity rt (200:1)
      endif
      if extcommunity rt matches-any (100:2) then
        set extcommunity rt (200:2)
      endif
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 200
     neighbor 30.1.19.1
      add vpnv4 uni
       route-policy R1_INBOUND i

# Option C mVPN | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-mvpn.md)
.

Load **russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.c.mvpn.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.c.mvpn.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.c.mvpn.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

**NOTE**: This is not working on CSR1000v 16.9.8. You will need to redeploy the topology with CSR100v version 17.x for this to work. This works on 17.3.2 for me.

L3VPN inter-AS option C is fully setup and working. Configure mVPN inter-AS using profile 11.

*   Use P-PIM in the core with SSM
    
    *   PIM is already enabled everywhere, including on the ASBR NNI links
        
    
*   Use BGP for C-multicast signaling
    
*   BGP ipv4/mvpn is already configured within each AS, but not for the RR-RR BGP session
    

On R1, join (192.0.2.1, 232.1.1.1) within VRF L3B and L3C. Ensure that when R1 VRF L3A pings this group, both 172.16.18.1 and 172.16.110.1 respond.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-mvpn#id-099854e6-f35c-497d-a9b5-2a9bed055560)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-mvpn#e3c6d0d5-5ed5-4ee0-a067-bda8e2c81c92)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In inter-AS option C, all PE and RR loopbacks are distributed into each AS. This allows mVPN to operate as normal, provided the core tree can be setup. In profile 11, we use P-PIM in the underlay, so all routers must have routes to the remote PE loopbacks in order to build the PIM distribution tree hop-by-hop.

In AS65002, we are using BGP-LU for remote loopback reachability. BGP-LU is needed here because we are using SR, so we cannot simply redistribute loopbacks into the IGP and rely on LDP to allocate a label. However, this presents a problem when R8 tries to join an SSM group such as (R6, 232.0.0.1). Its neighbors XR13 and R9 do not have a route to R6, so their RPF check fails. (Another option would be to use PIM RPF proxy, but this in my opinion is more complex than just extending iBGP-LU on all P routers).

To solve this, we can run BGP-LU in a full mesh, including the P routers.

Next, the RRs run ipv4/mvpn as an additional address-family on the eBGP session.

Finally, the PEs enable mVPN as usual. The only interesting note is the **inter-as** keyword, which prevents the NO\_EXPORT community from being attached to the BGP routes.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-mvpn#b127e82d-4138-48ac-8020-8166b1cce266)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On R8, verify that it has learned the auto-discovery routes for the remote PEs:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FIp6rlXfI7jX0c7DTgtoJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D96a6b112-8e5c-44bd-9e2f-0091bce62d09&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=20358ed15408b0ea91eb63c9d68a759a&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FkOc8Qh1YLsQ8dw3oqwQW%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D03c0759d-a998-4066-8671-105fc3ac0722&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=022b94491b6d3c51233f21c97b012704&sv=3)

R8 should join the SSM group in the P-PIM underlay:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnhcT6EbRHkapPHUoP42g%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D63be3845-65b6-4a1d-892e-49227acec7f7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d58f209a529068f31c2c820022129f80&sv=3)

The ASBRs should have SSM state for all four entries - one per PE. On R3 we see all four. The two remote PEs have an RPF neighbor of R2 given the lower MED we set in the previous lab.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhcpVTxhKp7zOANONytmJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc271da03-6fb3-450e-9e72-b2c054ccb25b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ad86b0e7cb48f6a3e5f3204e09ef6508&sv=3)

XR11 is the preferred egress for R8 and R10 within AS65001, so XR11 holds the state for these two entries:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVxRrgxZjKgUHAryRhSyQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8bc22070-abb6-4655-9f78-6cc3c206cdf6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=25d24a51d7513a86fd572cffea05b10b&sv=3)

R2 holds the state for the R6, XR12 rooted entries, with OIL including the NNI to R3:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FR8A3nvsB1mRxSkHblUqa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7769e041-ce48-4b05-8d8c-4e2a50597b1b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f0d1d49e99eeb283583297b162b1b284&sv=3)

The P-PIM underlay is simply built by enabling PIM everywhere and ensuring that every single router has a route to the remote PE loopbacks.

Next, the BGP service routes are reflected between the RRs just like VPN/v4/v6 and l2vpn/evpn. We’ll join an SSM group on R1 VRF L3B and L3C, which will prompt a type 7 route from R8 and R10.

XR12 receives the route from R10 (due to highest RID), and adds the (S, G) entry in the MRIB for the VRF, with the OIL including the tunnel for the default MDT. Remember that XR12 is the bestpath to 192.0.2.1 because it receives the route from R1 with lower MED.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0l8o62pOARbTbleClZ7u%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da4d807eb-2c9d-472d-9454-7e192c499a14&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=47d6a5116324e280dbb6184a5c18140d&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FEqIu6N76sYJzQ5FPiQ9G%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D600530f9-cb7a-4db9-9a8c-21b97e9b4d93&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=05b1944ca5d312f470e11500e2a72105&sv=3)

When R1 pings this group from L3A, both “hosts” in L3B and L3C respond.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FwiEy8rjoyq5Yivv0U3SH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcd7274c5-c87e-4ee5-9990-c77c0a0bcd68&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8cba429b52fc95db1a53c5e5111ce498&sv=3)

### Notes on mLDP as the underlay[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-mvpn#id-2eb41482-baa2-4ddf-b11c-7eb7fb1b2c6e)

mLDP can also easily be used for the underlay. You must enable mLDP everywhere (including the NNI). If using BGP-LU for the distribution of remote loopbacks (instead of redistributing into the IGP), then you also must enable recursive-FEC. This is only available on IOS-XR. There is a separate lab on this in the mVPN lab series using all IOS-XR routers.

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-mvpn#e3c6d0d5-5ed5-4ee0-a067-bda8e2c81c92)

      mdt default 232.0.0.1

       route-policy PASS out

     neighbor 10.0.0.9 use neighbor-group IBGP_RRC
     neighbor 10.0.0.13 use neighbor-group IBGP_RRC

     neighbor 10.0.0.14 remote-as 65002

      allocate-label all

# Option A mVPN | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-a-mvpn.md)
.

Load **russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.a.mvpn.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.a.mvpn.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.a.mvpn.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

L3VPN inter-AS option A is fully setup and working.

Enable mVPN using the following guidelines:

*   Use profile 1 in Globomantics (AS65001)
    
    *   mVPN default MDT MP2MP, with PIM as the overlay
        
    *   Use CSR7 as the root
        
    
*   Use profile 0 in Wired Brain (AS65002)
    
    *   P-PIM default MDT using PIM-BiDir, PIM as the overlay
        
        *   Use XR14 as the RP
            
        
    *   PIM is already enabled on all core interfaces
        
    

On R1, join (192.0.2.1, 232.1.1.1) within vrf L3B and L3C. Ensure that when R1 pings this group, both 172.16.18.1 and 172.16.110.1 respond.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-a-mvpn#id-6cccfe7d-6001-4dce-8254-7c2a74bbf88f)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-a-mvpn#c4f84554-95ed-4666-a615-fd7caf12f9f9)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Inter-AS option A for mVPN works very much the same as option A for unicast L3VPN. First, we must have a working inter-AS L3VPN setup anyways, as the AS with the receivers will need routes back to the sources in the other AS in order for the RPF check to work. Once the unicast L3VPN is setup correctly, the ASBRs simply treat each other as CEs for multicast traffic. It is simply a matter of enabling PIM on the ASBR links.

First we setup the mVPN in each AS. AS65001 uses profile 1 which involves C-PIM in the overlay and mLDP MP2MP in the underlay. Given that C-PIM overlay is the default, all we need to do is configure the mLDP root on each PE. We also make sure to enable PIM on all PE-CE links, including links towards ASBRs (which are treated as CEs in option A).

Next, AS65002 uses profile 0 with P-PIM in the underlay via PIM-BiDir, and C-PIM in the overlay via the multicast GRE tunnel.

We can verify that mVPN is working within each AS. R7 should see a mLDP MP2MP tree rooted at itself with several interested receivers:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXOBTgeazviOcO8T4DrxS%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da1f237c3-a89c-440d-be48-97920ba9acce&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0afe3c89a1f7c79e7b312028d6d2cab3&sv=3)

Any PE should see all other PEs as C-PIM neighbors.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FjXB2zOryMTGV7QkVWFkU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De9498ef9-070f-41bb-94bf-2be768f86445&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3a96febf1e2e83ce90dd433d993004da&sv=3)

Likewise in AS65002, we should see a PIM-BiDir tree rooted at XR14:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FdyMGzi4sq2asbDgBJtM2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Deaec6617-5360-44b6-9e16-eb3c3605fd13&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c89bc494137b8565058990bb1535320f&sv=3)

All PEs in AS65002 should also see each other as C-PIM neighbors:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbnZ8OaPWGjKYsw4iQsth%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D22477aea-fba1-43c7-b7a1-8d9a79317be8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0da314a0d464f7768184458fc62a7325&sv=3)

At this point, all that is needed is for the ASBRs to enable PIM on the NNI:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4VhbwnBDQSvsiIvBuYZf%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D812f5a3e-a549-420d-93a1-38e1d2e9139a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=962d1e01f4a6702f9b1e43a257465c1f&sv=3)

### Verifying multicast traffic[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-a-mvpn#fcf0d17a-ae5b-40c7-bb6a-72cc483dbdf6)

On R1, we’ll join (192.0.2.1, 232.1.1.1) within vrf L3B and L3C. Remember to enable IGMP v3 on the PEs.

Within AS65002, the PIM Joins make their way to R3, as the source is known via R3. R3 uses the interface towards R2 as the RPF interface, as the best BGP route is via R2.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fe4DoKJsX1mXKpuoGvZZj%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D57b0e31d-9616-4095-80db-ed38ac399c7b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b9578bb8e2d95e2db458b50e69284d89&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F3JS4cCJGgchILtVqhV0X%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc8b57650-bfe3-4fb7-8082-fe77c8036a19&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3fb4f65bb808b786f1ced931cba5ca8f&sv=3)

R2 receives the PIM Join from a “CE” and simply continues the process. R2 finds the best route is via XR12 (because R1 is setting MED high towards R6). The link to the ASBR/”CE” is added to the OIL. R2 has no idea that the “CE” is really an ASBR in another completely separate AS.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVouQghTXR7A8Afe25xnV%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dde27685b-9693-4426-9b91-81c35f626ffc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7701a86175d0fa6908f02380c1aba6f1&sv=3)

The (S, G) state makes its way to XR12, and the tree is successfully built. When R1 in VRF L3A pings the group, it receives replies from both hosts.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FQRMRd3EzbIfxzxDinsKQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2c65d82b-ab01-4537-a41c-513370005333&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=73874d402f323be0243bbe36e013a33c&sv=3)

In summary, mVPN with Option A is simply a matter of enabling PIM on the L3 NNI. As long as mVPN is independently working in each AS, and unicast inter-AS is working, then mVPN should be working as well.

    # Globomantics (AS65001)
    # 
    #XR11, XR12
    vrf L3A
     vpn id 65000:101
    !
    multicast-routing add ipv4 int lo0 en
    multicast-routing vrf L3A add ipv4
     interface all enable
     mdt so lo0
     mdt default mldp ipv4 10.0.0.7
    !
    route-policy USE_MLDP
     set core-tree mldp-default
    end-policy
    !
    router pim vrf L3A add ipv4
     rpf topology route-policy USE_MLDP
    !
    mpls ldp mldp
    
    #R6
    vrf definition L3A
     vpn id 65000:101
     add ipv4
      mdt default mpls mldp 10.0.0.7
    !
    ip multicast-routing vrf L3A distributed
    ip pim vrf L3A ssm default
    !
    int GigabitEthernet2.3016
     ip pim sparse-mode
    
    #R2
    vrf definition L3A
     vpn id 65000:101
     add ipv4
      mdt default mpls mldp 10.0.0.7
    !
    ip multicast-routing vrf L3A distributed
    ip pim vrf L3A ssm default
    !
    int Gi2.233777
     ip pim sparse-mode
    
    # Wired Brain (AS65002)
    #
    #R3, R4, R8, R9, R10
    ip multicast-routing distributed
    int lo0
     ip pim sparse-mode
    ip pim bidir-enable
    
    #XR13
    multicast-routing add ipv4 int all en
    
    #XR14
    multicast-routing add ipv4 int all en
    router pim add ipv4 bsr candidate-rp 10.0.0.14 bidir
    router pim add ipv4 bsr candidate-bsr 10.0.0.14
    
    #R3
    ip multicast-routing vrf L3BC distributed
    ip pim vrf L3BC ssm default
    !
    vrf definition L3BC
     address-family ipv4
      mdt default 239.0.0.1
    !
    int Gi2.233777
     ip pim sparse-mode
    int Gi2.3113888
     ip pim sparse-mode
    
    #R8
    ip multicast-routing vrf L3B distributed
    ip pim vrf L3B ssm default
    !
    vrf definition L3B
     address-family ipv4
      mdt default 239.0.0.1
    !
    int GigabitEthernet2.3018
     ip pim sparse-mode
    
    #R10

    ip pim vrf L3C ssm default
    !
    vrf definition L3C

# Notes - CoPP (IOS-XE) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-copp-ios-xe.md)
.

Control plane policing (CoPP) is essentially just the ability to apply a policy-map to the router’s CPU. The idea is that control plane and management plane traffic are processed in the CPU, so overwhemling the router with control/mgmt plane traffic can be a form of DoS attack. To protect against this, we can limit this traffic using MQC style QoS policies that are applied to the CPU itself.

For example, the following config limits control plane protocols to 20 pps, Telnet to 10 pss and ICMP to 5 pps.

Copy

    ip access-list ext ROUTING-PROTOCOLS-ACL
     permit tcp any any eq 179
     permit tcp any eq 179 any
     permit ospf any any
    !
    class-map ROUTING-PROTOCOLS-CM
     match access-group name ROUTING-PROTOCOLS-ACL
    !
    !
    ip access-list ext MGMT-PROTOCOLS-ACL
     permit tcp any any eq 23
     permit tcp any eq 23 any
    !
    class-map MGMT-PROTOCOLS-CM
     match access-group name MGMT-PROTOCOLS-ACL
    !
    !
    ip access-list ext ICMP-ACL
     permit icmp any any
    !
    class-map ICMP-CM
     match access-group name ICMP-ACL
    !
    !
    policy-map COPP
     class ROUTING-PROTOCOLS-CM
      police rate 20 pps
     class MGMT-PROTOCOLS-CM
      police rate 10 pps
     class ICMP-CM
      police rate 5 pps
    !
    control-plane
     service-policy input COPP

The policy-map counters can be verified as follows:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FHjyLek2v6agC3113Shgm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3dbcdac2-ee20-4016-9984-5cd364d6e59f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bccaf50facef25fcad234f9b910575e5&sv=3)

We can see that ICMP is rate limited to 5 pps. The burst value is 1 which seems to explain why only one ping gets through per second:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FLbGEpo2C2a2aTbfcVHAh%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7a487957-59ea-4d7d-b7c3-335b2ec8cb29&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=273c1d14f810a590c0ba23450d129059&sv=3)

In summary, CoPP is simply the practice of applying QoS policing to the CPU, as if the CPU was a virtual interface.

### CoPP vs. MPP[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-copp-ios-xe#ec919868-0b73-489d-a5f2-cd44b4c4e7f8)

With MPP there is more risk, since you can lock yourself out of an interface or protocol entirely.

With CoPP, it seems safer because you can let packets hit the class-default and permit. You also have more granular control in terms of source IP and rate limiting instead of completely dropping. But you have to be careful with CoPP because it impacts routing protocol traffic, while MPP does not.

[PreviousNotes - MPP (IOS-XE)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-mpp-ios-xe)

# Option C L3NNI | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-l3nni.md)
.

Load **russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.c.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.c.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:russo.pl.course.inter-as.opt.c.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure inter-AS option C using the following guidelines:

*   Globomantics is AS65001 and Wired Brain is AS65002
    
*   Globomantics has two ASBRs. Configure MED on XR11 and R2 so that R2 is used for ingress. R3 has **bgp bestpath med missing-as-worst** configured. Do not change this.
    
*   In AS65001, redistribute the BGP-LU routes into the IGP, and IGP routes into BGP-LU. Set the metric so that XR11 is the preferred egress point for remote loopbacks. Ensure that routing loops cannot occur.
    
*   In AS65002, use iBGP-LU for advertisement of transport labels for the remote PEs/RR
    

All IGP/BGP peerings are already setup (except for the ASBR-ASBR peerings for option C).

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-l3nni#b36880fc-0d7e-4b6a-8268-3d040193a738)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-l3nni#cb3982e5-1717-48f5-8f97-9533d0f0ab9b)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Inter-AS option C provides even more scalability by removing the VPN tables on the ASBRs. Instead, the ASBRs simply share loopbacks of their PEs and RRs. This is used to extend BGP services between the ASs. The RRs form a BGP session to reflect service routes, and the PEs will have remote PEs loopbacks in their RIB in order to form end-to-end LSPs.

AS65002 is simpler, so we will start there. There is only one ASBR, which is R3. The AS will run iBGP-LU instead of having the ASBR redistribute the routes into the IGP. This is more scalable than poluting the IGP with external routes. Plus, AS65002 is using SR, so this would not work anyways, as the routers would not allocate a label for these redistributed prefixes.

Within AS65002, each PE and RR simply advertises its own loopback into BGP-LU. A label is allocated, but by default imp-null will be allocated, as the PE itself owns the prefix. However, this allows R3 to then allocate its own label for the prefix, as it is setting next-hop-self to the ASBRs on the NNI.

XR14 does the same, and enables IPv4/LU for the iBGP RR peers.

Next, AS65001 runs BGP-LU on the NNI as well. R2 sets the MED outbound to a lower number than XR11. This is done to demonstrate the need for the **set mpls-label** command on IOS-XE. When you use an outbound route-map on a BGP IPv4/LU peer, you must include this command. Otherwise, the MPLS label is stripped. You can however _not_ use an outbound route-map without any issues. But if you do use an outbound route-map, you must include this **set** statement.

R2 and XR11 also redistribute loopbacks from the IGP into BGP. They deny tag 20 to prevent route redistribution loops.

Additionally, R2 and XR11 redistribute the BGP routes into the IGP directly. They set the tag which prevents route feedback when ISIS routes are advertised back into BGP. XR11 sets the metric lower so that egress traffic uses XR11 instead of R2.

Now that both ASs have each other’s loopbacks, the RRs can form an eBGP session and exchange any needed VPN service routes. Remember to use **next-hop-unchanged** so that the RRs are not inserted into the data path, and also do not allocate their own VPN labels.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-l3nni#ad59ba98-e8c3-41a2-86fa-8f1d011fcb05)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Within AS65001, we see routes for the remote loopbacks via the IGP. XR11 is preferred as egress:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOMh2e44zkmUeazZYhkJN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De56aca49-0543-4c75-bed2-96c4e97e3ddf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b6a0777e5c159cddbd55de1f593669ed&sv=3)

Within AS65002, the PEs and RRs know the remote loopbacks via BGP-LU.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrNvfe3COZnNXIct43067%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df5eb2d56-d55b-4370-b449-dcede6799e0d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ea039c3f82a7bdd888352d809057aaca&sv=3)

The result is that traffic from AS65002 will be transported to R3 with a top label of 16003, and a bottom label of the BGP label that R3 allocated for each prefix.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FxsqFNBjhRQRCMtunds8w%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2c90eb7c-6db2-4ac6-8b01-b996afaae166&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=36bde8f5dcea2760020fdecbc373433c&sv=3)

However, traffic from AS65001 to AS65002 only needs a single transport label, as the loopbacks are redistributed directly into IGP, where LDP allocates labels. In AS65002, BGP-LU is essentially another service, so R8 needs to tunnel traffic to R3, as the AS65002 core is “BGP-LU free.”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FYEWIYznTdL2i26f9Tb2T%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df3ac9d80-0ddd-453d-91b6-bec3752b9728&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=15b144b62fdf1d59f3f6dfec72389a42&sv=3)

Let’s now look at BGP services. R6 has VPNv4 and VPNv6 routes that have nexthops of R8 and R10. This is because the RR is doing **next-hop-unchanged**. This gives the “feel” of all PEs being within the same AS. Once you accomplish inter-AS loopback transport, VPN services simply resolve to the real PE loopbacks.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FU5xeUVj0M1uRw4KNdTxy%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8f411767-5b3d-4d01-8fe9-0795bac17775&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0906785968a269bf3d22579dba8acb3b&sv=3)

Similarly, R8 and R10 have routes pointing to XR12 (which is the bestpath due to lower MED advertised by R1 in L3A) and R6.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsF374owXpagvxT9LumS4%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dbac2b525-51e1-41b4-91b8-98093ddbdea9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cd48a985177b5554db9b1fc474c646c4&sv=3)

A traceroute from L3A to L3B reveals at most two labels. This is because AS65001 does not need to use an extra transport label in the core due to redistributing BGP-LU routes directly into the IGP.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FpZ1nHwksD7d0l8O47oOm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3fb2107f-ecf2-4bba-ae09-ff6f21526d8f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d33358e1248f52c0ede3dbf37f9ce827&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FX7FeCdBSOHGSSHX2lztU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D21496f5e-e729-4571-8703-08073faacbf2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=14eada8dff9c435fc71f57d2afe86257&sv=3)

A traceroute in the other direction produces a three-label stack within AS65002 due to the extra transport label.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F20ErQOrAO7SruaS1g3TE%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2b4aaf50-4c7d-4810-aeb2-6db5dd9b3105&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f7cc8b36cb4622872b5e4e46d9088f06&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKRRnJsTPlCa2ObEYFKia%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D70a00c9e-9fcc-4159-9be1-71321678cff4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=560ba6a72169b9aa61b4281fb8db0480&sv=3)

Summary[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-l3nni#c65053bc-c43d-4f4e-a244-ca8124917e56)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Inter-AS option C is somewhat more simplistic than option B. The ASBRs are simply used to advertise PE/RR loopback reachability. This must have a label associated with it so that the LSP can work end-to-end. BGP-LU is used to allocate a label for each prefix. Just like option B, we must be careful to enable MPLS on the NNI. This involves a static route on IOS-XR, and ensuring the **mpls bgp forwarding** command exists on the NNI on IOS-XE.

Once the loopback reachability is established, the RRs run an eBGP session with the nexthop unchanged to propagate service routes between the ASs. From there, the PEs will preform normal VPN service operations, finding the service label from the BGP route, and transporting the traffic to the remote PE using either the IGP or BGP-LU to find the transport label.

As a summary:

*   Option A uses a per-VRF subinterface on the NNI. The ASBRs treat each other as CEs.
    
    *   This is characterized by an unlabeled hop at the NNI.
        
    
*   Option B uses VPNv4/v6 sessions between the ASRBs. The ASBRs must allocate a local label for every VPN route advertised to the remote ASBR over the NNI.
    
    *   This is characterized by a single-labeled hop at the NNI.
        
    *   There are either two or three VPN labels in the end-to-end path. If the ASBR sets next-hop-self on the iBGP session to the RR, there are three VPN labels.
        
    
*   Option C uses BGP-LU sessions between the ASRBs. The ASBRs only need to allocate a local label per PE/RR which is very scalable. The RRs run an eBGP session with next-hop-unchanged. The PEs can then form a complete end-to-end LSP.
    
    *   This is characterized by a double-labeled hop at the NNI.
        
    *   The AS has the option to redistribute the remote BGP-LU prefixes into IGP, using LDP to bind labels, or extend iBGP-LU to all PEs. If extending iBGP-LU, you will see a three-label stack in that AS. Top label is transport to the ASBR. Middle label is service label for the iBGP-LU prefix representing the remote PE. Bottom label is the final VPN label learned from the remote PE.

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-l3nni#cb3982e5-1717-48f5-8f97-9533d0f0ab9b)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-l3nni#ad59ba98-e8c3-41a2-86fa-8f1d011fcb05)
    
*   [Summary](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/russo-inter-as/option-c-l3nni#c65053bc-c43d-4f4e-a244-ca8124917e56)
    

Copy

    #R2
    ip prefix-list HOST_ROUTES permit 10.0.0.0/8 ge 32
    !
    route-map ISIS_TO_BGP deny 10
     match tag 20
    route-map ISIS_TO_BGP permit 20
     match ip addr prefix HOST_ROUTES
    !
    route-map BGP_TO_ISIS permit 10
     set tag 20
    !
    route-map SET_MED
     set metric 10
     set mpls-label
    !
    router isis 65001
     redistribute bgp 65001 metric 200 route-map BGP_TO_ISIS
    !
    router bgp 65001
     neighbor 10.2.3.3 remote-as 65002
     add ipv4
      redistribute isis 65001 route-map ISIS_TO_BGP
      neighbor 10.2.3.3 activate
      neighbor 10.2.3.3 route-map SET_MED out
      neighbor 10.2.3.3 send-label
     
    #XR11
    router static add ipv4 uni
     10.3.11.3/32 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.3113888
    !
    route-policy ISIS_TO_BGP
     if tag eq 20 then
      drop
     endif
     if destination in ( 0.0.0.0/0 ge 32 ) then
      pass
     endif
    end-policy
    !
    route-policy BGP_TO_ISIS
     set tag 20
    end-policy
    !
    route-policy SET_MED($MED)
     set med $MED
    end-policy
    !
    route-policy PASS
     pass
    end-policy
    !
    router isis 65001
     add ipv4
      redistribute bgp 65001 metric 100 route-policy BGP_TO_ISIS
    !
    router bgp 65001
     add ipv4 unicast
      redistribute isis 65001 route-policy ISIS_TO_BGP
      allocate-label all
     !
     neighbor 10.3.11.3
      remote-as 65002
      add ipv4 labeled-uni
       route-policy SET_MED(20) out
       route-policy PASS in
    
    #R7
    router bgp 65001
     neighbor 10.0.0.14 remote-as 65002
     neighbor 10.0.0.14 update-so lo0
     neighbor 10.0.0.14 ebgp-multihop
     !
     add vpnv4
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 activate
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 next-hop-unchanged
     add vpnv6
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 activate
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 next-hop-unchanged
    
    
    
    #R3
    router bgp 65002
     neighbor 10.2.3.2 remote-as 65001
     neighbor 10.3.11.11 remote-as 65001
     add ipv4
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 act
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 send-label
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 next-hop-self
      neighbor 10.2.3.2 act
      neighbor 10.2.3.2 send-label
      neighbor 10.3.11.11 act
      neighbor 10.3.11.11 send-label
    
    #R8
    router bgp 65002
     add ipv4
      network 10.0.0.8 mask 255.255.255.255
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 act
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 send-label
    
    #R10
    router bgp 65002
     add ipv4
      network 10.0.0.10 mask 255.255.255.255
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 act
      neighbor 10.0.0.14 send-label
    
    #XR14
    route-policy PASS
     pass
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 65002
     add ipv4 uni
      network 10.0.0.14/32
      allocate-label all
     !
     neighbor-group IBGP_RRC
      add ipv4 labeled-unicast
       route-reflector-client
     !
     neighbor 10.0.0.7
      remote-as 65001
      update-so lo0
      ebgp-multihop
      !
      add vpnv4 uni
       route-policy PASS in
       route-policy PASS out
       next-hop-unchanged
      add vpnv6 uni
       route-policy PASS in
       route-policy PASS out
       next-hop-unchanged

# Notes - WAN MACsec Config Guide | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-wan-macsec-config-guide.md)
.

[https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/ios-xml/ios/macsec/configuration/xe-16/macsec-xe-16-book/wan-macsec-mka-support-enhance.html](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/ios-xml/ios/macsec/configuration/xe-16/macsec-xe-16-book/wan-macsec-mka-support-enhance.html)

The dot1q tag in the clear feature allows EVPLs to work, and also allows for QoS to be applied on a per-VLAN basis using the CoS field that is now visible in the 802.1Q tag.

Both MACsec and non-MACsec subinterfaces can co-exist on the same physical interface.

Both 128 and 256 bit AES-GCM encryption is available for data packets. Both 128 and 256 bit AES-CMAC encryption is available for control packets.

MTU overhead with MACsec is 32 bytes. (16 byte SEC tag and 16 byte ICV trailer). It is recommended to explicitly configure the interface MTU to adjust for this.

You can use **macsec access-control should-secure|must-secure** to control whether unencrypted packets from the physical interface or subinterfaces are allowed.

*   **should-secure** means that unencrypted packets are allowed
    
*   **must-secure** means that unencrypted packets are not allowed
    
    *   The default setting is **must-secure**
        
    
*   The **should-secure** command can only be configured at the interface level
    
*   If you will have non-MACsec subinterfaces, you need to configure **should-secure** on the physical interface
    

Replay protection is a feature of MACsec which prevents replay attacks. Each packet is given a unique sequence number, and the remote end verifies the sequence number. However, a SP network might reorder packets. In this case we can define a window which allows a given number of packets to be received out of order. The default setting is 64. We control this using **macsec replay-protection window-size**.

WAN MACsec can work on an E-LAN service. There is no difference - you just make sure all CEs have the same PSK.

[PreviousNotes - WAN MACsec White Paper](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-wan-macsec-white-paper)

# Start | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/inter-as-l3vpn/start.md)
.

These labs use INE's topology from their SPv4 workbook.

To begin, run the following command on your containerlab machine:

Copy

    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    containerlab deploy -t ine-spv4/ine-spv4.clab.yml --reconfigure

Once all nodes are started, run the following command to transfer the config files to all nodes. These files will be used to change between startup configs for subsequent labs.

Copy

    python3 transfer_configs_to_nodes.py

The script will prompt you for a directory name. Enter "ine-spv4".

Use the MTPutty session file located in **ine-spv4/ine-spv4\_putty\_sessions.xml** to quickly setup your SSH sessions to the nodes. Go to **Server - Import Tree** and browse for the file.

When you are done with the lab, use the following command to wipe it:

Copy

    containerlab destroy -t ine-spv4/ine-spv4.clab.yml

# Notes - LPTS (IOS-XR) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-lpts-ios-xr.md)
.

LPTS (Local Packet Transport Service) is a process running on each line card that is responsible for transporting “for\_us” traffic to the correct destination (typically either the linecard CPU or RP).

LPTS uses a pre internal FIB table (pifib) table that determines where to send each flow. For example, ARP, BFD, ICMP, and OAM traffic is sent to the line card CPU. LDP, BGP, OSPF, etc. traffic is sent to the RP CPU. LPTS also plays a role in NSR by punting traffic to both RPs at the same time.

LPTS comes with default policing values so that traffic cannot overwhelm the CPUs on the router. We can tune these individually per flow type using:

Copy

    lpts pifib hardware police flow <flow type> rate <pps>

The values can be confirmed using **show lpts pifib hardware police**

### Example[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-lpts-ios-xr#id-08dd3642-fe1e-4b6e-8d31-0f8e25364a4d)

Let’s examine the default values for LDP traffic:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fc6MpeaPpzTL5qmGS4gLX%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd342a8a0-3fe9-4686-a7c6-593187b0d557&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7165632a71d6b52516b1f93d092c1e7a&sv=3)

LDP has four different flow types: TCP for a known peer, a configured peer, and the default TCP rate, as well as a UDP rate. A known peer is an established TCP session. A configured peer is a TCP session that is not established, but a flow that matches a configured peer.

We can set these rates individually using:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzO2ROzTNwwwMFQdXEgiA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D05342269-c236-4027-8f39-fac1c2751288&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=66083599830b256b3824d28fb4c88491&sv=3)

The average rate type changes to global because we configured these rates globally in the CLI.

Remember that only control plane traffic is subjected to these policing values, because only for\_us traffic will be inspected by the LPTS. Data plane traffic passes through the interfaces without inspection from LPTS.

### Further Reading[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-lpts-ios-xr#b33c5ff7-f545-421a-be76-de9f9f2c74a8)

[https://ccnp-sp.gitbook.io/studyguide/security/lpts-local-packet-transport-services](https://ccnp-sp.gitbook.io/studyguide/security/lpts-local-packet-transport-services)

[https://community.cisco.com/t5/service-providers-knowledge-base/asr9000-xr-local-packet-transport-services-lpts-copp/ta-p/3123792/show-comments/true](https://community.cisco.com/t5/service-providers-knowledge-base/asr9000-xr-local-packet-transport-services-lpts-copp/ta-p/3123792/show-comments/true)

[PreviousNotes - CoPP (IOS-XE)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-copp-ios-xe)
[NextNotes - WAN MACsec White Paper](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-wan-macsec-white-paper)

*   [Example](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-lpts-ios-xr#id-08dd3642-fe1e-4b6e-8d31-0f8e25364a4d)
    
*   [Further Reading](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/security/notes-lpts-ios-xr#b33c5ff7-f545-421a-be76-de9f9f2c74a8)
    

Copy

    lpts pifib hardware police
     flow ldp tcp known rate 300
     flow ldp tcp configured rate 500
     flow ldp tcp default rate 100
     flow ldp udp rate 100
